Which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}),$ for $t>0?$
questions.worked_solution:
The definition of $\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{{(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t})}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1}{4{t}^{2}}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}{4{t}^{2}}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\sqrt{{(\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t})}^{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+|\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}|)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ we have $\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}>0,$ and we can remove the absolute value in the above expression. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2t}+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{2t}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2{t}^{2}}{2t}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $f(x)=\operatorname{tanh}⁡({x}^{2})$  and $x\ge 0,$ calculate  ${f}^{-1}(x)$ from first-principles.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{tanh}⁡{x}^{2}.$ Note that $f(x)$ is a one-to-one function on $x\ge 0.$ We have $y\in [0,1)$ for $x\in [0,\infty ).$ 

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡{y}^{2},
$$

where $x\in [0,1)$ and $y\in [0,\infty ).$

Next, we apply the definition of $\operatorname{tanh}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{e}^{2{y}^{2}}-1}{{e}^{2{y}^{2}}+1} \\ x({e}^{2{y}^{2}}+1) & ={e}^{2{y}^{2}}-1 \\ (x-1){e}^{2{y}^{2}} & +(x+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the ${e}^{2{y}^{2}}$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{y}^{2}} & =-\frac{x+1}{x-1} \\ {e}^{2{y}^{2}} & =\frac{1+x}{1-x} \\ 2{y}^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x}) \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x}) \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ we select the positive root. Therefore,

$$
y=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1+x}{1-x})}.
$$

questions.problem:
Using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x-3)$ and $x\ge \frac{3}{2}.$

${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡($
{{field-1}}$)+$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x-3).$ Since $x\ge \frac{3}{2},$ we have $y\ge 1.$

To find the inverse function, we swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2y-3),
$$

where $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge \frac{3}{2}.$

Next, we apply the definition of hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\,({e}^{2y-3}+{e}^{-(2y-3)}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{2y-3}+{e}^{-(2y-3)} \\ 2x{e}^{2y-3} & ={e}^{4y-6}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{4y-6}-2x{e}^{2y-3}+1 & =0 \\ ({e}^{2y-3})^{2}-2x({e}^{2y-3})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{2y-3}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{2y-3} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ 2y-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\le 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\ge 1.$ Since $2y-3\ge 0,$ the logarithm in the above equality must be positive, so we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}) \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})+3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})+\frac{3}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Using the definition of the hyperbolic sine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\sqrt{x})$ for $x\ge 0.$

${f}^{-1}(x)=($
{{field-1}}$)^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡\sqrt{x}.$ Note that $f(x)$ is a one-to-one function on its entire domain. We have $y\in [0,\infty )$ for $x\in [0,\infty ).$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
x=\operatorname{sinh}⁡\sqrt{y},
$$

where $x\in [0,\infty )$ and $y\in [0,\infty ).$

Next, we apply the definition of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{\sqrt{y}}-{e}^{-\sqrt{y}}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{\sqrt{y}}-{e}^{-\sqrt{y}} \\ 2x{e}^{\sqrt{y}} & ={e}^{2\sqrt{y}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the right-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\sqrt{y}}-2x{e}^{\sqrt{y}}-1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{\sqrt{y}})}^{2}-2x({e}^{\sqrt{y}})-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{\sqrt{y}}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ {e}^{\sqrt{y}} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \sqrt{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ y & ={ln}^{2}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we require real $y$ and $x<\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}$ for all $x,$ we select the positive solution. Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}))}^{2}.
$$

\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(y-2)^{2}}-2x{e}^{(y-2)^{2}}+1 & =0 \\ ({e}^{(y-2)^{2}})^{2}-2x({e}^{(y-2)^{2}})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{(y-2)^{2}}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{(y-2)^{2}} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\le 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\ge 1.$ Since the logarithm in the above equality must be positive, we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}) \\ y-2 & =\pm \sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})} \\ y & =2\pm \sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want $y\ge 2,$ select the positive solution. Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})}+2.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The hyperbolic functions have inverse functions that are easy to define. The **inverse hyperbolic functions** are the following:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

- The **inverse hyperbolic sine**, defined as

$$
\sinh^{-1}{x} = \arsinh{x} = \ln\big(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\big), \qquad x \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

The graph of the inverse hyperbolic sine function is given below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189991/assets/1f07f38b11cf297e099341df2ab062d4691c4502098c060de565b70f1ea7e360.png)

- The **inverse hyperbolic cosine**, defined as

$$
\cosh^{-1}{x} = \arcosh{x} = \ln\big(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\big), \qquad x \in [1, \infty).
$$

The graph of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is given below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189991/assets/60607a764c50807dcb0f4f05328d900c626079654995cffbaa84fa2214788835.png)

- The **inverse hyperbolic tangent**, defined as

$$
\tanh^{-1}{x} = \artanh{x} = \dfrac12\ln\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right), \qquad x \in (-1, 1).
$$

The graph of the inverse hyperbolic tangent function is given below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189991/assets/96b4f7aa06ee165751dcaa2101e9dea104d95d5bebdaea7bc4f317d9160b5a7a.png)

For example, to calculate $\arcosh(\sqrt2)$ we substitute $x$ for $\sqrt2$ in the formula for $\arcosh$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\sqrt{2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}-1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2-1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Deriving the Formulas for the Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
tutorials.problem:
We can derive the formulas from inverse hyperbolic sine, cosine, and tangent from the definition of these base functions. 

For example, let's show that
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\cosh^{-1}{x} = \arcosh{x} = \ln\big(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\big), \qquad x \in [1, \infty).
$$

Recall that

$$
\cosh{x} = \dfrac12 \left( e^x + e^{-x} \right).
$$

First, let $y = \cosh{x}$ and $x \geq 0.$ Then we have $y\geq 1.$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, now we have that $x \geq 1$ and $y \geq 0.$

Next, we use the definition of $\cosh x$ and bring everything to the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{y}+{e}^{-y}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{y}+{e}^{-y} \\ 2x{e}^{y} & ={e}^{2y}+1 \\ {e}^{2y}-2x{e}^{y}+1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{y})}^{2}-2x({e}^{y})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Letting $Y = e^{y},$ we form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{y} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{x^{2}-1}\leq 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{x^{2}-1}\geq 1.$ Since $y \ge 0,$ the logarithm in the above equality must be positive, so we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain our formula for $\arcosh{:}$

$$
f^{-1}(x)=
\arcosh{x} = \ln\big(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\big).
$$
